name: Lavender
partsUsed: flowers, flowering tops, leaves, essential oil
description: A silver-leaved Mediterranean shrub crowned in violet spikes whose scent seems to quiet the whole garden. Romans scented their baths with it, which gave the plant its name from the Latin lavare, 'to wash.' Medieval folk strewed it on floors and tucked it into linens, and witches have long burned it to call peace into troubled houses.
metaphysicalUses: Lavender is the great soother of the herbal cupboard. Burn it or hang it to bring calm and gentle happiness to a home, scatter it through love sachets to attract kind and lasting affection, and add it to cleansing baths to wash away anxiety and petty negativity. Cunningham notes it was once worn to see ghosts and that its scent attracts men, while old lore holds that lavender sprinkled on the head with rosemary preserves chastity. It is a favored herb for sleep and dream pillows, for Midsummer fires, and for any working that asks the mind to grow still enough to listen.
medicalUses: Traditionally a gentle nervine, lavender has been taken as a mild tea or inhaled to ease restlessness, tension headaches and sleeplessness. The diluted essential oil is a classic folk remedy for minor burns, insect bites and small scrapes, and it has long been massaged into temples for headache. Herbalists also used it as a carminative for nervous digestion and windy stomachs.
whereToFind: Native to the western Mediterranean hills, on dry, rocky, sunny slopes. It grows easily in gardens in full sun with lean, well-drained soil; harvest flower spikes just as the lowest buds open, on a dry morning, and hang in bundles to dry. Plants are sold at nearly every garden center, and dried buds and essential oil are available from apothecaries, health food stores and herb suppliers.
uses: Tuck dried buds under your pillow or in a dream sachet for peaceful sleep
Add a handful of flowers to a ritual bath to wash away stress before spellwork
Burn dried lavender as incense to bring calm into a house after an argument
Steep a mild tea of the buds to sip before meditation
Add to love sachets and honey jars for gentle, kind affection
Hang bundles over the doorway to welcome peace and good spirits
Dab diluted oil on the temples to soothe a tension headache
caution: Generally safe in culinary and mild tea amounts; oral use can cause nausea, headache or burping. Never swallow the essential oil, and always dilute it before skin use, since some people develop allergic skin reactions. A few cases of breast swelling have been reported in children using lavender skin products, so avoid regular use of lavender oil products on children. Use cautiously in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and stop medicinal use 2 weeks before surgery because it may add to sedation.
interactions: May add to the effects of sedatives, sleep medicines, benzodiazepines and alcohol.
pets: Lavender is toxic to dogs, cats and horses (nausea, vomiting, poor appetite); keep the plant and especially the essential oil away from pets, and do not diffuse it around cats.

name: Rosemary
description: A resinous, needle-leaved evergreen of sea cliffs, its pale blue flowers said to have taken their color when the Virgin Mary spread her cloak over the bush. 'There's rosemary, that's for remembrance,' says Ophelia, and the herb was carried at both weddings and funerals. Old English lore says that where rosemary flourishes, the woman rules the house.
metaphysicalUses: Rosemary is one of the oldest cleansing and protective herbs, a ready substitute for frankincense in incense, and was burned in sickrooms and temples alike. Hang it at the door or plant it by the gate to keep thieves and ill-wishers away, and place it under the pillow to guard against nightmares. It strengthens memory and focus in study spells, is worn for remembrance of the dead, and is woven into love and fidelity charms. A rosemary wash or bath purifies before ritual, and a sprig in a wand or broom bundle sweeps out stagnant energy.
medicalUses: Traditionally a warming, stimulating herb taken as a tea for poor circulation, sluggish digestion and fatigue, and famed in folk belief for sharpening memory. Infused rosemary oil was rubbed into sore muscles and aching joints, and rosemary rinses were used for dandruff and to encourage hair growth. Its antiseptic qualities made it a traditional wash for small wounds and a fumigant in sickrooms.
whereToFind: Native to the coastal Mediterranean, growing on dry, sunny cliffs and scrub near the sea. It thrives in pots or sunny, well-drained beds and can be overwintered indoors in cold climates; snip sprigs any time of year, ideally just before flowering for strongest oil. Fresh sprigs are sold in grocery stores, plants at garden centers, and dried leaf and oil at apothecaries.
uses: Burn dried rosemary as a cleansing smoke or in place of frankincense
Hang a sprig above the front door for protection against thieves and ill will
Keep a sprig on your desk or tuck it behind the ear while studying for memory
Add rosemary to a ritual bath before spellwork for purification
Lay a sprig on a grave or ancestor altar for remembrance
Make a rosemary hair rinse to strengthen hair and spirit together
Place under the pillow to ward off nightmares
caution: Safe in culinary amounts. Avoid medicinal doses and the essential oil in pregnancy (it can stimulate menstrual flow) and with epilepsy or a seizure history, since the camphor-rich oil may trigger seizures. Use caution with bleeding disorders and stop medicinal use 2 weeks before surgery. Never ingest the essential oil, dilute it for skin use, and do not use the oil on or near the faces of infants and young children.
interactions: Medicinal amounts may add to the effects of blood thinners (warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel) and may interfere with ACE inhibitors, diuretics and lithium.
pets: Keep the essential oil away from pets, especially cats; do not diffuse it where a cat cannot leave the room.

name: Sage
description: A soft, grey-green, velvety-leaved herb whose Latin name comes from salvere, 'to be saved' or 'to heal.' A medieval proverb asked, 'Why should a man die whilst sage grows in his garden?' It has been the wise-woman's herb of longevity, sound judgment and household cleansing for centuries.
metaphysicalUses: Garden sage is an herb of wisdom, immortality and protection. Old lore says to eat a little in May for long life, and that sage thrives in a garden when its owner's business prospers. Write a wish on a sage leaf and sleep with it beneath your pillow for three nights; if you dream of the wish it will come true, and if not, bury the leaf. Burn it to cleanse a space, carry it to protect against the evil eye, and add it to money workings for wise and steady prosperity. It is also used to honor elders and seek counsel from the grandmothers.
medicalUses: Sage tea is a classic traditional gargle for sore throats, mouth ulcers and inflamed gums, and was taken warm for colds and to ease heavy sweating, including hot flushes. It has long been used as a digestive bitter after rich, fatty meals and was believed to strengthen memory in old age. Its astringent, antiseptic leaves were applied to small wounds.
whereToFind: Native to the Mediterranean and Balkans, growing on dry, sunny, rocky ground. It is an easy perennial in full sun and well-drained soil; harvest leaves before flowering for best flavor and dry them in loose bunches. Find plants at garden centers, fresh bunches at grocers, and dried leaf from apothecaries and herb shops.
uses: Write a wish on a leaf and sleep with it under your pillow for three nights
Burn dried leaves to cleanse a room, a practice open to all traditions
Gargle a cooled sage tea for a sore throat
Add sage to money and business jars for wise, steady prosperity
Carry a leaf in a pocket for protection and good judgment
Place sage on an ancestor altar to honor elders and wise women
caution: Safe in culinary amounts. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy and breastfeeding (it is traditionally used to dry up milk). Sage contains thujone, which can cause seizures and other toxic effects in large or prolonged doses; do not take high doses long-term, never ingest the essential oil, and avoid medicinal amounts with epilepsy or seizure disorders. Medicinal amounts may lower blood sugar and may affect blood pressure. Burn only in a well-ventilated room, away from babies, pets and anyone with asthma, and never leave it smoldering unattended.
interactions: Medicinal amounts may add to the effects of diabetes medicines and sedatives, and could reduce the effectiveness of anticonvulsant (seizure) medicines.

name: White Sage
description: A pale, almost moon-white shrub of the coastal sage scrub of Southern California and Baja California, its silvery leaves heavy with a sharp, resinous fragrance. It is a sacred plant to many Indigenous peoples of the region, including the Chumash, Tongva, Kumeyaay and Cahuilla, who have used it in ceremony and healing for generations. Its popularity in the wider world has led to overharvesting and poaching from wild lands.
metaphysicalUses: White sage is renowned for its strong purifying smoke, used to clear heavy or stagnant energies from spaces, tools and people. For practitioners outside the Indigenous traditions that hold it sacred, the respectful path is to work with ethically grown or Native-sourced plants, or to choose alternatives such as garden sage, rosemary, juniper, cedar, mugwort or local herbs. Many witches grow their own white sage and use a single leaf as a gentle offering or in protection sachets rather than burning large bundles.
medicalUses: Among Indigenous Californian peoples, white sage has traditionally been used as a tea or steam for colds and congestion, as a wash, and its leaves rubbed on the body. In folk herbal use it is regarded as antiseptic and drying. These are cultural traditions and should be respected as such.
whereToFind: Native to coastal sage scrub and chaparral of Southern California and northern Baja California, on dry, sunny slopes. Do not forage it from the wild, where it is often poached. Grow it yourself in very well-drained soil and full sun in dry climates, or buy from Native-owned businesses and ethical growers who cultivate it.
uses: Grow a plant and use single fallen leaves as a gentle cleansing offering
Keep a cultivated leaf in a protection sachet
Choose ethical, cultivated sources or Native-owned sellers when buying
Substitute garden sage, rosemary, juniper or cedar for routine space clearing
Learn about and support the Indigenous communities who hold this plant sacred
caution: Do not ingest in quantity; there is little safety data, so avoid internal use during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Like all burned plant material, the smoke releases fine particles that irritate the lungs; burn only in a well-ventilated room and avoid it around asthma, lung disease, infants and pets. Never leave a smoldering bundle unattended and extinguish it fully in sand or a fireproof dish. Ethical note: wild white sage is overharvested and culturally significant; avoid wild-harvested stock.
pets: Keep smoke away from pets, especially birds and cats, whose airways are sensitive.

name: Mugwort
description: A tall, silver-backed roadside herb sacred to Artemis, goddess of the moon and wild places. Anglo-Saxons named it the eldest of the Nine Sacred Herbs, and Roman soldiers lined their sandals with it against weariness on long marches. The undersides of its leaves shimmer like moonlight, and it has long been the witch's herb of dreams and second sight.
metaphysicalUses: Mugwort opens the inner eye. Burn it with sandalwood or wormwood during scrying, wash crystal balls and mirrors in its infusion, and stuff dream pillows with it to provoke vivid, prophetic dreams and lucid travel. It is carried for protection on journeys, laid in shoes against fatigue, and hung over doors on Midsummer Eve to keep away evil. Mugwort is a lunar, oracular herb and a natural ally for full-moon work, tarot readings and spirit communication.
medicalUses: A traditional bitter digestive used in small amounts to stimulate appetite and ease bloating, and in old European herbals to bring on delayed menstruation and soothe cramps. It is the herb burned in moxibustion in East Asian medicine. Leaves were also once used in brewing before hops.
whereToFind: Native across temperate Europe, Asia and North Africa and naturalized widely in North America, growing on roadsides, waste ground and riverbanks, often abundantly. Harvest the leafy tops just before or as they flower in late summer and hang to dry. Dried mugwort is sold by herb suppliers, apothecaries and Asian markets (as moxa or 'ssuk').
uses: Fill a small dream pillow with dried mugwort for prophetic dreams
Wash scrying mirrors and crystal balls in a cooled mugwort infusion
Burn a pinch with sandalwood before tarot or divination
Lay a leaf in your shoe on long journeys for strength and protection
Hang a bundle over the door on Midsummer Eve against harm
Bundle mugwort into smoke wands as an alternative to white sage
caution: Avoid completely in pregnancy (it may stimulate the uterus and harm the fetus) and while breastfeeding. Mugwort is in the daisy family and is a major pollen allergen; it can cause allergic reactions in people sensitive to ragweed, chrysanthemum, dandelion, sunflower, or with mugwort pollen and related food allergies (such as celery, carrot and spices). Contains thujone; not for long-term or heavy internal use. Smoke from burning or moxa can irritate the lungs, so ventilate well.
interactions: Interactions are not well studied; check with a healthcare provider before combining medicinal amounts with prescription medicines.

name: Yarrow
description: A feathery-leaved meadow herb with flat white umbels, named for Achilles, who was said to stanch his soldiers' wounds with it at Troy. Its dried stalks were used in China to cast the I Ching, and in Europe young lovers slept on it to dream of their true love. It has been found in a Neanderthal burial, making it one of humanity's oldest companions.
metaphysicalUses: Yarrow is worn for courage and protection, and carried to attract friends and distant loved ones. Called 'Seven Year's Love,' it is hung over the marriage bed and given at weddings to ensure the couple stays happy for seven years. Pick a sprig while reciting the old rhyme, then sleep on it to dream of a future spouse. Its infusion washed over the head is said to prevent headaches and over the eyes to enhance psychic sight, and the stalks are traditional for I Ching divination. Yarrow also strengthens boundaries for empaths and sensitives.
medicalUses: Known as Soldier's Woundwort, yarrow leaves were packed into cuts to slow bleeding and help them heal. A hot tea was a classic folk remedy to bring on a sweat and break a fever at the start of a cold, often combined with elder flower and peppermint. It was also used as a bitter digestive and to ease heavy or painful menstruation.
whereToFind: Native throughout the temperate Northern Hemisphere, growing in meadows, field edges, lawns and roadsides. Harvest the flowering tops in summer when the flowers are fully open, and dry in bunches. Seed and plants are available from garden centers and wildflower nurseries; dried herb from apothecaries.
uses: Carry a sprig for courage before a difficult conversation
Hang dried yarrow over the bed of newlyweds for seven years of love
Sleep on a sprig to dream of your true love
Use dried stalks for I Ching or simple yes/no casting
Sip a hot yarrow, elder and peppermint tea at the first sign of a cold
Dab the closed eyelids with a clean cloth dipped in cooled, freshly made infusion before divination (skip this if you are allergic to the daisy family)
Add to protection sachets for empaths and sensitive folk
caution: Avoid in pregnancy and while breastfeeding; it contains small amounts of thujone and has been used to bring on menstruation. Contact dermatitis is the most common reaction, and people allergic to the daisy (Aster) family should avoid it, including near the eyes. Very large amounts (several cups a day) have caused side effects. Avoid medicinal amounts with bleeding disorders and stop 2 weeks before surgery.
interactions: May add to the effects of blood thinners, diuretics (water pills), lithium and sedatives.
pets: Yarrow is listed by the ASPCA as toxic to dogs, cats and horses (vomiting, diarrhea, drooling, poor appetite, skin irritation, depression).

name: Chamomile
description: A low, sweet, apple-scented plant whose little white-and-gold flowers look like tiny suns. The Egyptians dedicated it to the sun and prized it above other herbs, and the Anglo-Saxons counted it among their Nine Sacred Herbs. It is called the 'plant's physician,' because sickly plants were said to recover when chamomile grew beside them.
metaphysicalUses: Chamomile is a gentle sun herb for peace, sleep and good fortune. Gamblers wash their hands in its tea to win, and in hoodoo it is a classic lucky herb for money drawing. Burn it or drink it to bring sleep and meditative calm, add it to bath magic to attract love, and sprinkle it around a property to remove curses and spells cast against you. Its soft, solar energy is ideal for children's blessings and for workings that ask for success without strain.
medicalUses: One of the most beloved folk remedies, chamomile tea has been taken for generations to ease nervous tension, restlessness, sleeplessness and colicky, upset stomachs. Cooled tea and compresses were used for sore eyes, irritated skin, rashes and minor inflammations, and the flowers were added to baths for soothing achy bodies.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and western Asia, growing in fields, sunny waste places and disturbed ground. Easy to grow from seed in sunny beds; pick the flowers when fully open on dry days and dry them on screens. Dried flowers and tea bags are available from grocers, health food stores and apothecaries.
uses: Brew a cup of chamomile tea before bed for peaceful sleep
Wash your hands in chamomile tea before games of chance for luck
Add flowers to a money-drawing sachet or green candle spell
Sprinkle chamomile around your property to break curses
Pour a strong infusion into a bath to attract love and ease tension
Use a cooled tea bag as a compress on closed, tired, puffy eyes (skip this if you are allergic to ragweed or daisies)
caution: Likely safe in tea amounts, but avoid if allergic to ragweed, daisies, marigolds or chrysanthemums; rare severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported. Using chamomile near the eyes can cause irritation. Little is known about safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so keep to moderate tea amounts. It may have mild estrogen-like effects, so avoid medicinal amounts with hormone-sensitive conditions.
interactions: Interactions with warfarin (increased bleeding risk) have been reported; may add to sedatives and alcohol, may affect some liver-metabolized drugs such as cyclosporine, and may reduce the effectiveness of birth control pills.
pets: Chamomile is listed by the ASPCA as toxic to dogs, cats and horses (skin irritation, vomiting, diarrhea, allergic reactions; bleeding tendencies with long-term use).

name: Peppermint
description: A vigorous, cool-burning hybrid of water mint and spearmint, its square stems and fierce aroma unmistakable. Greek myth tells of the nymph Minthe, transformed into the plant by jealous Persephone, while Pluto softened the curse by giving her a sweet scent. Romans crowned themselves with mint at feasts and ancient Egyptians placed it in tombs.
metaphysicalUses: Peppermint is a bright, energizing purifier. Rub fresh leaves on furniture, walls and floors to clear negativity, and add it to healing and purification incenses. Smelling it is said to promote sleep, while sleeping with a leaf under the pillow may give a glimpse of the future. Peppermint is also used in money and travel spells, and in hoodoo it is a quick-acting herb added to formulas to speed results. Its Mercurial energy sharpens the mind for study and clear communication.
medicalUses: Peppermint tea is a time-honored remedy for indigestion, gas, nausea and colicky stomachs. Its vapor was inhaled for stuffy heads and colds, and diluted oil was rubbed on temples for tension headaches and on aching muscles for its cooling effect.
whereToFind: A cultivated hybrid originating in Europe, now naturalized in damp places, streambanks and ditches in many temperate regions. It spreads aggressively, so grow it in a pot; harvest leaves just before flowering for the strongest oil. Fresh mint is in grocery stores, plants at garden centers, and dried leaf and oil at apothecaries.
uses: Rub fresh leaves on doorframes and furniture to clear stagnant energy
Sip peppermint tea after a heavy meal for digestion
Add to money-drawing powders to quicken results
Inhale a peppermint steam to clear the head before study or divination
Tuck a leaf in your wallet to draw money
Add a few fresh leaves to a cleansing floor wash
caution: Tea is generally safe, but peppermint may worsen heartburn and acid reflux. Never apply peppermint oil to the face, chest or near the nose of infants and young children, as menthol can cause breathing problems. Do not swallow the essential oil (only enteric-coated capsules are taken internally, under guidance), and always dilute it for skin use. Use caution with gallbladder disease or gallstones.
interactions: Peppermint oil may raise levels of cyclosporine and some other liver-metabolized drugs; antacids and acid reducers can make enteric-coated peppermint capsules dissolve too early and cause heartburn.
pets: Mint is listed by the ASPCA as toxic to dogs, cats and horses (vomiting, diarrhea); peppermint essential oil is especially dangerous to cats, so do not diffuse it around them.

name: Spearmint
description: The gentler, sweeter cousin of peppermint, with spear-shaped leaves and a soft green fragrance. It is the mint of mint sauce, mint juleps and Moroccan tea, and was strewn on the floors of medieval churches and halls. Pliny wrote that its scent 'stirs up the mind,' and it was used in ancient Greek baths and funeral rites.
metaphysicalUses: Spearmint carries a softer, more Venusian energy than peppermint and is used in healing spells, especially those for the lungs and chest. Its scent sharpens the mind and is said to protect during sleep. Place spearmint in sachets and jars for love and money, add it to gentle home blessings, and burn it in healing incense. It is a lovely herb for workings that need sweetness and clarity together.
medicalUses: Spearmint tea has long been used as a mild remedy for indigestion, nausea, hiccups and gas, and is gentle enough to have been given to children in folk practice. It was also taken for colds and sore throats as a pleasant warming-cooling tea.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and southern Asia and naturalized widely in moist ground, ditches and streamsides. Grow in containers to keep it from spreading; pick leaves through the growing season. Fresh bunches are sold at grocery stores and markets, and dried leaf at apothecaries and tea shops.
uses: Brew a sweet spearmint tea for gentle digestion
Place leaves in a healing sachet for a loved one
Add to love jars for sweetness and clear-hearted affection
Keep a sprig near your bed for protection during sleep
Add to money-drawing baths for prosperity
Strew fresh leaves in a home blessing ritual
caution: Generally safe in food and tea amounts. Large amounts may aggravate reflux, and large amounts of spearmint tea may worsen kidney or liver disease and should be avoided in pregnancy. Do not ingest the essential oil, dilute it for skin use, and keep the oil away from the faces of infants and young children.
interactions: Large amounts may add to the drowsiness of sedative medicines and increase the risk of liver harm with liver-toxic drugs (such as acetaminophen, methotrexate, some statins and antifungals).
pets: Mint is listed by the ASPCA as toxic to dogs, cats and horses (vomiting, diarrhea); keep the essential oil away from cats.

name: Basil
description: A fragrant, glossy-leaved herb whose name comes from the Greek basileus, 'king.' In Italy a pot of basil on the windowsill once signaled a woman ready to receive her suitor, and in India its sacred cousin tulsi is honored as a goddess. Basil has long been a herb of love and protection in Mediterranean and Caribbean folk magic.
metaphysicalUses: Basil is a powerful herb of love, wealth and protection. Carry it in a wallet or place it in the cash register to draw money and customers, and sprinkle it on the floor or in a floor wash to bring prosperity into a business. Its scent is said to cause sympathy between two people, and it soothes quarrels between lovers. It is worn to keep a partner faithful, scattered to protect a home, and in Vodou basil is sacred to Erzulie and used in her love workings.
medicalUses: Traditionally a warming, carminative culinary herb used to ease gas, bloating and mild stomach cramps. Fresh leaves were rubbed on insect bites and stings, and basil tea was given for nausea and nervous headaches.
whereToFind: Native to tropical Asia and Africa. Grow from seed after the last frost in full sun and rich soil; pinch the tops to keep it bushy and harvest before it flowers. Fresh plants and bunches are sold at grocers and garden centers; dried basil at any spice shop.
uses: Tuck a few leaves in your wallet or cash drawer to draw money
Add basil to a prosperity floor wash for your shop or office
Share a basil-scented meal with a partner to soothe a quarrel
Grow a pot by the front door for protection and luck
Scatter dried basil in love sachets for fidelity
Rub a fresh leaf on a mosquito bite to ease the itch
caution: Safe in culinary amounts. Basil contains estragole, which in high, long-term doses has caused liver tumors in animals, so avoid concentrated medicinal doses and the essential oil in pregnancy, breastfeeding and in children. Basil essential oil should not be ingested and must be diluted for skin use. Basil oils and extracts may slow blood clotting and lower blood pressure and blood sugar, so avoid them with bleeding disorders and stop medicinal amounts 2 weeks before surgery.
interactions: Medicinal amounts or extracts may add to the effects of blood thinners and antiplatelet drugs (warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel) and blood pressure medicines.
pets: Keep the essential oil away from pets, especially cats; do not diffuse it where a cat cannot leave the room.

name: Thyme
description: A tiny, woody, sun-loving herb whose fragrant leaves hum with bees all summer. Greek warriors bathed in thyme for courage, and medieval ladies embroidered a bee upon a sprig of thyme on scarves for their knights. English folklore holds that wild thyme beds are where the fairies dance, and that wearing thyme lets one see them.
metaphysicalUses: Thyme is an herb of courage and purification. Burn it to cleanse a space, and take a spring bath of marjoram and thyme to wash away the sorrows of the past. Wear a sprig to strengthen courage and bravery, place it under the pillow to ward off nightmares and ensure restful sleep, and wear it in the hair to become irresistible. Thyme is also a key herb for faery work: grow a patch for the Fair Folk and wear the flowers on Midsummer to perceive them.
medicalUses: Thyme is a traditional remedy for coughs, chest colds, bronchitis and sore throats, taken as a tea sweetened with honey or as a syrup. Its strongly antiseptic qualities made it a wash for wounds and a gargle for the mouth and throat. It was also used to ease gas and stomach cramps.
whereToFind: Native to the western Mediterranean, growing on dry, stony, sunny hillsides. Easy to grow in pots or rock gardens with full sun and sharp drainage; harvest sprigs just before flowering. Fresh and dried thyme are sold at every grocer; plants at garden centers.
uses: Wear or carry a sprig for courage before a challenge
Burn thyme as a purifying incense before ritual
Make a thyme and honey syrup for winter coughs (never give honey to babies under 1 year)
Plant a thyme bed as a dancing ground for the Fair Folk
Bathe in marjoram and thyme in spring to release old sorrow
Tuck a sprig under your pillow against nightmares
caution: Safe in culinary amounts; stick to food amounts in pregnancy and breastfeeding. People allergic to oregano or other mint-family plants may react to thyme. Medicinal amounts may slow blood clotting and act like estrogen, so avoid them with bleeding disorders or hormone-sensitive conditions (breast, uterine or ovarian cancer, endometriosis, fibroids) and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Thyme essential oil is strong and irritating; dilute it well, never ingest it, and keep it away from the faces of young children. Never give honey or honey-based syrups to babies under 1 year old (risk of infant botulism). Burn only in a well-ventilated room, away from babies, pets and anyone with asthma, and never leave it smoldering unattended.
interactions: Medicinal amounts may add to blood thinners and antiplatelet drugs (warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel, NSAIDs), may interfere with estrogen therapy, and may interact with anticholinergic and cholinergic drugs, including Alzheimer's medicines such as donepezil.
pets: Keep the essential oil away from pets, especially cats; do not diffuse it where a cat cannot leave the room.

name: Bay Laurel
description: A glossy-leaved evergreen tree sacred to Apollo, whose beloved nymph Daphne was transformed into a laurel to escape him. Victors and poets were crowned with its wreaths, and the Pythia at Delphi chewed bay leaves or breathed their smoke before prophesying. Old lore says lightning never strikes a bay tree.
metaphysicalUses: Bay is the herb of victory, prophecy and wish-making. Write a wish on a bay leaf and burn it, or carry it until the wish comes true. Place leaves under the pillow for prophetic dreams, burn them to induce visions, and wear them as an amulet against negativity and evil. Bay leaves in the corners of a room protect a house, and in hoodoo they are added to legal and success workings for triumph over enemies. Sweep with a branch of bay for cleansing, or crown yourself with a wreath on days you must shine.
medicalUses: Bay leaves are a traditional culinary digestive, cooked into stews and soups to ease heaviness and gas. In folk practice an infused bay oil was rubbed into aching joints and sore muscles. Leaves are always removed before eating.
whereToFind: Native to the Mediterranean, growing on scrubby hillsides and in damp, shady ravines. It can be grown as a shrub in mild climates or in a large pot overwintered indoors; pick leaves at any time. Dried bay leaves are found in every spice aisle; trees in larger garden centers and nurseries.
uses: Write a wish on a bay leaf and burn it safely in a fireproof dish
Place a leaf under the pillow for prophetic dreams
Put bay leaves in the four corners of a room for protection
Carry a bay leaf in your wallet before a court date or interview for victory
Add bay to cleansing floor washes and protection jars
Weave a bay wreath to crown yourself on a day of success
caution: Use only true bay (Laurus nobilis); some plants called 'laurel' (cherry laurel, mountain laurel) are poisonous. Never swallow whole leaves: they do not soften and can lodge in the throat or injure the gut, so remove them before eating. Medicinal amounts may affect blood sugar and cause drowsiness; avoid them in pregnancy and breastfeeding and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Burning leaves can irritate the lungs, so ventilate well and burn wish leaves only in a fireproof dish away from anything flammable. Some people develop contact dermatitis.
interactions: Medicinal amounts may add to the effects of diabetes medicines, sedatives and narcotic pain medicines.
pets: Bay laurel is listed by the ASPCA as toxic to dogs, cats and horses (vomiting, diarrhea); keep leaves away from pets.

name: Cinnamon
description: The curled, sweet, fiery inner bark of tropical trees, once more precious than gold. Egyptians used it in embalming and temple incense, and Herodotus repeated fantastical tales of great birds that built nests of cinnamon sticks. Its warm scent fills witches' kitchens with the energy of the sun.
metaphysicalUses: Cinnamon is a high-vibration fire spice that speeds and strengthens any working. Burn it in incense to raise spiritual vibrations, aid healing, draw money and stimulate psychic powers. Blow cinnamon through the front door on the first of the month to call in prosperity, an increasingly beloved modern folk ritual. It is added to love and lust sachets, used in success and business formulas, and stirred clockwise into teas and foods to draw abundance. In hoodoo, it is a common ingredient in money and luck oils.
medicalUses: A traditional warming spice used to ease indigestion, gas, nausea and loose bowels, and taken as a hot drink to warm cold hands and feet and fend off chills and colds. Folk herbalists also used it to support healthy circulation.
whereToFind: Native to Sri Lanka (true cinnamon) and southern China (cassia), grown in tropical plantations where the bark is peeled from coppiced shoots. It cannot be grown outdoors in temperate climates. Sticks and ground cinnamon are in every grocery store; Ceylon cinnamon from spice merchants and apothecaries.
uses: Blow a pinch of ground cinnamon through your front door on the first of the month (blow it away from your face and never inhale the powder)
Stir cinnamon clockwise into morning coffee while visualizing success
Add a stick to money jars and green candle spells
Burn cinnamon in incense to raise energy and speed a working
Simmer cinnamon sticks with orange peel to fill the home with warmth
Sprinkle in love and lust sachets for passion
caution: Cassia cinnamon contains coumarin, which in large regular amounts can harm the liver, especially in people with liver disease; prefer Ceylon cinnamon for frequent use and avoid high-dose supplements. Do not inhale or try to swallow dry ground cinnamon by the spoonful, which can choke and damage the lungs. Cinnamon essential oil is a strong skin irritant and sensitizer; never use it undiluted or on sensitive skin. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy and stop them 2 weeks before surgery. Burn only in a well-ventilated room, away from babies, pets and anyone with asthma, and never leave it smoldering unattended.
interactions: Medicinal amounts may lower blood sugar and add to diabetes medicines; cassia's coumarin may add to liver harm from liver-toxic drugs, and large amounts may increase bleeding risk with blood thinners.
pets: Cinnamon powder in large amounts, inhaled powder, and especially cinnamon essential oil can harm pets; keep the oil away from cats and dogs.

name: Clove
description: The dried, nail-shaped flower buds of an evergreen tree from the Maluku 'Spice Islands,' whose name comes from the Latin clavus, 'nail.' Han dynasty courtiers held cloves in their mouths to sweeten their breath before addressing the emperor. Wars were fought over the trade, and the scent still carries something royal and fierce.
metaphysicalUses: Clove is burned in incense to attract riches, drive away hostile and negative forces, and purify the surroundings. Worn or carried, it attracts the opposite sex and comforts the bereaved. Cloves strung on a red thread make a protective charm, and a clove-studded orange pomander is a classic winter talisman for luck and love. Hoodoo practitioners use clove to stop gossip and to command friendship, and in Jupiterian money magic it draws abundance and influence.
medicalUses: Clove oil is the classic folk remedy for toothache, dabbed sparingly on the sore gum for its numbing, antiseptic effect. Cloves were also used as a warming digestive to ease gas, nausea and vomiting, and chewed to freshen the breath.
whereToFind: Native to the Maluku Islands of Indonesia, grown on tropical plantations where the buds are picked before opening and sun-dried. Whole cloves are available in any spice aisle; clove oil from pharmacies and apothecaries.
uses: Make a clove-studded orange pomander for winter luck and love
String cloves on red thread as a protective charm
Burn cloves on charcoal to drive away negativity
Add whole cloves to money jars and prosperity sachets
Hold cloves in a sachet to stop gossip against you
Dab a tiny drop of diluted clove oil on a sore gum while waiting for the dentist
caution: Clove essential oil is very strong and can burn skin, gums and mucous membranes; dilute it and use only a tiny amount, briefly. Clove oil is dangerous for children: even small amounts swallowed can cause seizures, liver damage and fluid imbalances, so never use it for teething and keep the bottle out of reach. Eugenol slows blood clotting and cloves may affect blood sugar, so avoid medicinal amounts with bleeding disorders and in pregnancy, and stop 2 weeks before surgery. If burning on charcoal, do it only in a well-ventilated room on a heatproof surface, never in a closed space, because burning charcoal gives off carbon monoxide.
interactions: Clove may increase bleeding with blood thinners and antiplatelet drugs, may add to diabetes medicines, and may alter the breakdown of some liver-metabolized drugs.
pets: Clove oil is toxic to cats and harmful to dogs; never apply it to pets or diffuse it around cats.

name: Nutmeg
description: The hard, marbled seed of an evergreen tree from Indonesia's Banda Islands, wrapped in a crimson lace-like aril that becomes mace. Its trade drove colonial wars and made fortunes; the Dutch famously traded Manhattan for the nutmeg island of Run. In English folk magic a whole nutmeg is a lucky charm carried by gamblers and the hopeful.
metaphysicalUses: Nutmeg is a lucky charm. Carry a whole nutmeg as an amulet for good fortune, especially in games of chance, and string nutmegs with star anise and tonka beans for a classic luck necklace. Grated into money powders and green candles it draws prosperity, and it is used in fidelity spells and to strengthen clairvoyance. In hoodoo it is a known gambling herb, often anointed with a lucky oil and carried in a mojo bag.
medicalUses: In tiny culinary amounts, nutmeg is a traditional warming digestive that eases gas, nausea and loose bowels. A pinch grated into warm milk is an old folk remedy for sleeplessness.
whereToFind: Native to the Banda Islands of Indonesia, grown on tropical plantations in Grenada, India and Indonesia. Not cultivable outdoors in temperate climates. Whole nutmegs are best bought from spice shops and grocers; grate fresh as needed.
uses: Carry a whole nutmeg in your pocket for luck when gambling
Grate a pinch into a green candle spell for prosperity
Add a whole nutmeg to a gambler's mojo bag
Grate a tiny pinch into warm milk before bed
String with star anise for a good-luck garland
Add to fidelity sachets for a steady, faithful heart
caution: Use only culinary pinches. Larger amounts (roughly 2 teaspoons, about 5 grams, or more) can cause serious poisoning from myristicin, with hallucinations, racing heart, nausea, agitation and anxiety lasting a day or two, and deaths have been reported; never use nutmeg recreationally. Avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Keep whole nutmegs away from children and pets.
interactions: Large amounts may add to the effects of sedatives and other drugs acting on the nervous system.
pets: Recipe amounts are unlikely to harm pets, but a large amount (such as a whole nutmeg) can cause hallucinations, fast heart rate and seizures in dogs and cats.

name: Star Anise
description: A star-shaped, eight-pointed seed pod from an evergreen tree of southern China and Vietnam, with a sweet, licorice scent. Its perfect geometry makes it a natural talisman, and it has been burned in Buddhist temples and placed on graves in Japan. Each pod is a little compass of luck.
metaphysicalUses: Star anise is burned as incense to increase psychic powers and is worn or carried as a pendulum or amulet. A pod placed at each of the four directions consecrates a sacred space. Strung on a thread or carried in a pocket, it draws luck, and pods are often found on the altar during divination. Grind the seeds to add to incense for spiritual awareness and to purify tools.
medicalUses: Star anise is a traditional warming culinary spice used in East Asian cooking and folk medicine to ease gas, bloating and colic, and as an ingredient in remedies for coughs and colds. It is a natural source of shikimic acid.
whereToFind: Native to southern China and northeast Vietnam, grown on plantations. Not hardy outdoors in cold climates. Buy whole pods from Asian grocers, spice shops and supermarkets; choose intact eight-pointed stars for charms.
uses: Place a pod at each of the four quarters to consecrate a ritual space
Carry a whole star in your pocket for luck
Burn ground star anise with mugwort before divination
Use a pod on a string as a simple pendulum charm
Simmer pods in mulled cider for warmth and good fortune
Add to protection sachets and luck garlands
caution: Use only Chinese star anise (Illicium verum) from a reputable food-grade source. Japanese star anise (Illicium anisatum) looks almost identical and is poisonous, and teas have been found contaminated with it; the FDA has warned against star anise teas. Never give star anise teas to infants or young children, as seizures, severe vomiting and irritability have been reported. People allergic to anise, fennel, celery, carrot, birch or mugwort may react. Avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Burn only in a well-ventilated room, away from babies, pets and anyone with asthma, and never leave it smoldering unattended.

name: Ginger
description: A knobbly, golden, fiery rhizome cultivated in tropical Asia for thousands of years. It was among the first spices carried west along the trade routes, and medieval Europeans believed it came from the Garden of Eden. In the kitchen witch's hands, ginger is the spark that lights a spell.
metaphysicalUses: Ginger heats up and speeds any working, which is why it is added to spells to give them power. Eat ginger before casting to fill yourself with fiery energy, and add it to money jars, success spells and love workings for quick results. In the Pacific, ginger is chewed and spat at the sea for protection from storms. Whole roots can be planted and tended as a living money spell: as the plant grows, so grows your wealth.
medicalUses: Ginger is a famous traditional remedy for nausea, motion sickness and morning queasiness. Hot ginger tea with honey and lemon is a folk standard for colds, chills and sore throats, and ginger has long been used to warm the body, improve circulation, ease gas and soothe menstrual cramps and achy joints.
whereToFind: Native to tropical Southeast Asia, grown in warm, humid regions in rich, moist soil. It can be grown in pots from grocery-store roots in a warm, bright spot. Fresh roots are in every supermarket, and dried ground ginger in any spice aisle.
uses: Sip hot ginger tea before spellwork to stoke your inner fire
Add a slice of dried ginger to a money jar to speed results
Plant a ginger root in a pot as a living money spell
Chew candied ginger to settle a queasy stomach on journeys
Add powdered ginger to love and passion sachets
Grate fresh ginger into a warming bath for chills and vitality
caution: Safe in food amounts. Large medicinal doses may cause heartburn, gas and diarrhea, and may slow blood clotting; avoid medicinal amounts with bleeding disorders and stop 2 weeks before surgery. In pregnancy, use only moderate amounts for short periods and consult a healthcare provider. Use caution with gallstones, and do not put fresh ginger in a bath if you have sensitive or broken skin, as it can irritate.
interactions: Medicinal amounts may add to the effects of blood thinners and antiplatelet drugs (warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel) and may add to diabetes and blood pressure medicines.

name: Garlic
description: The pungent, papery-skinned bulb that has guarded homes and bodies across nearly every culture. Garlic was left at crossroads as an offering to Hecate, fed to the builders of the pyramids for strength, and famously hung against vampires in Eastern European lore. Its ferocious scent is both medicine and shield.
metaphysicalUses: Garlic is a supremely protective herb. Braids of garlic hung in the kitchen or over the door guard the home against evil spirits, envy and thieves, and a clove carried on the person protects on journeys. It is rubbed on pots and pans to remove negative influences that might contaminate food, and offered at the crossroads to Hecate. Peeled cloves placed in a room absorb illness and negativity and are then disposed of away from the home. Garlic also lends courage and stamina.
medicalUses: Garlic is one of the oldest traditional remedies, eaten raw or in honey to fight colds, coughs and infections and to support immunity. It was used as a folk antiseptic and antifungal, and is traditionally eaten to support healthy circulation and the heart.
whereToFind: Native to Central Asia and cultivated worldwide. Plant individual cloves in autumn in sunny, well-drained soil and harvest bulbs in midsummer when the lower leaves yellow. Bulbs are available everywhere from grocers and farmers' markets.
uses: Hang a braid of garlic in the kitchen to guard the home
Leave a garlic clove at a crossroads as an offering to Hecate on the dark moon
Carry a clove in your pocket when traveling for protection
Place peeled cloves in a sickroom to absorb illness, then bury them away from home
Make garlic honey for winter colds (never give honey to babies under 1 year)
Rub a cut clove around windowsills to block hostile energy
caution: Food amounts are safe, but medicinal amounts and supplements can thin the blood; avoid them with bleeding disorders and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Raw garlic can upset the stomach and can cause chemical burns if left on the skin, so do not apply it directly to skin. Garlic-in-oil must be refrigerated and used within a few days (or frozen) to prevent botulism; never store it at room temperature. Never give honey or honey-based syrups to babies under 1 year old (risk of infant botulism).
interactions: Garlic may increase bleeding with warfarin and other blood thinners, and garlic supplements greatly reduce blood levels of the HIV drug saquinavir and may affect other HIV medicines.
pets: Garlic is toxic to dogs and cats (it damages red blood cells, causing anemia), even in cooked or powdered form; never feed it to pets.

name: Rose
latin: Rosa spp. (Rosa damascena, Rosa gallica, Rosa canina)
partsUsed: petals, buds, hips, essential oil, rosewater
description: The queen of flowers, sacred to the love goddesses of every age. Roman banquets were showered with petals, Persian poets wrote of the nightingale's love for the rose, and secrets spoken 'sub rosa,' beneath the rose, were sworn never to be repeated. Its thorns remind us that love also guards itself.
metaphysicalUses: Rose is the heart of love magic. Rosebuds and petals are added to love sachets, baths, incense and teas to attract romance, and a rose-petal bath restores self-love and soothes a broken heart. Drinking rosebud tea before bed is said to bring prophetic dreams, and rosewater cleanses the aura and sacred tools. The thorny stems guard boundaries in protection spells, and rose hips strung as beads draw love. Rose is also used to calm household tempers and to raise the gentle vibrations needed for healing.
medicalUses: Rose petals and rosewater have long been used as a gentle astringent for the skin, to soothe inflamed eyes and as a fragrant uplift for low spirits and nervous tension. Rose hips, rich in vitamin C, were made into syrups for winter colds and immune support, and rose-petal infusions were used for sore throats.
whereToFind: Wild roses grow across the temperate Northern Hemisphere in hedgerows, woodland edges and thickets; dog rose hips can be foraged after the first frost. Grow fragrant old garden roses in sun and rich soil; pick petals in the morning after the dew dries. Use only unsprayed roses (florist roses are heavily treated); buy food-grade dried petals and rosewater from apothecaries.
uses: Take a rose-petal bath to restore self-love after heartbreak
Add dried rosebuds to love sachets and honey jars
Sip rosebud tea before bed for prophetic dreams
Mist rosewater over your aura or altar to cleanse and sweeten
Wrap a rose thorn in red thread as a guardian of the heart
Make rose-hip syrup for winter vitality
Lay petals in a circle around a pink candle for romance
caution: Use only organic or unsprayed roses for anything eaten, drunk or applied to skin. The fine hairs inside rose hips are irritating and must be strained out. Rose hips are rich in vitamin C, so people with kidney stones, iron overload (hemochromatosis) or on dialysis should check with a provider before regular medicinal use. Rose essential oil must be diluted. Rose thorns can carry fungi and bacteria, so wear gloves when handling and clean any puncture.
interactions: Rose hip supplements may interact with some statins and chemotherapy drugs; check with a provider before combining.

name: Jasmine
latin: Jasminum officinale; Jasminum grandiflorum; Jasminum sambac
description: A twining vine of starry white flowers that release their intoxicating scent most strongly after dark. In India it is woven into garlands for the gods and brides, and its perfume is called the 'Queen of the Night.' Jasmine belongs to the moon, to night-blooming dreams and to love that awakens slowly.
metaphysicalUses: Jasmine attracts spiritual love, as opposed to purely physical passion, and its flowers are added to love sachets and incense. Carry or burn it to draw wealth and money, and burn it in the bedroom to bring prophetic dreams. Its scent induces sleep and is a beautiful offering on the full moon. Jasmine oil is used to anoint candles for romance and for moon goddesses, and jasmine tea is sipped before divination.
medicalUses: In folk traditions, jasmine-scented tea and the scent of the flowers have been used to lift low spirits, ease nervous tension and relax the body. Jasmine oil, highly diluted, has been used in perfumery and skincare for dry or sensitive skin.
whereToFind: Native to the Himalayas, China and South Asia, growing as a climbing vine in warm, sheltered spots. Grow common jasmine on a sunny trellis in mild climates or indoors in pots; pick flowers at dusk when the scent is strongest. Jasmine tea is found at tea shops and Asian grocers; jasmine absolute at perfumers and apothecaries.
uses: Burn dried jasmine in the bedroom for prophetic dreams
Anoint a white or pink candle with jasmine oil on the full moon for spiritual love
Sip jasmine green tea before tarot reading
Add dried flowers to a money-drawing sachet
Float fresh blossoms in a moon-water bowl as an offering
Grow a vine by the bedroom window to sweeten night dreams
caution: Use only true Jasminum species. Carolina or yellow jessamine (Gelsemium sempervirens) and night-blooming jessamine (Cestrum) are poisonous and should never be eaten, drunk or burned. Jasmine absolute is potent and can sensitize the skin; dilute well and patch test. Jasmine green tea contains caffeine. Avoid medicinal use in pregnancy. Burn only in a well-ventilated room, away from babies, pets and anyone with asthma, and never leave it smoldering unattended.
pets: True jasmine is listed by the ASPCA as non-toxic to pets, but Carolina jessamine is highly toxic to animals; keep the absolute away from cats.

name: Calendula
description: A cheerful orange-gold flower that opens with the morning sun and closes at dusk, earning it the name 'Husbandman's Dial.' Its name comes from the Latin calendae, the first day of each month, for it was said to bloom every month of the year. Medieval folk dedicated it to Mary and hung garlands over doors to keep evil from entering.
metaphysicalUses: Calendula is a sun herb of protection and happiness. Garlands of marigold strung over doorposts stop evil from entering, and flowers scattered under the bed protect while you sleep and bring prophetic dreams. Carry the petals into court for a favorable outcome, and add them to spells for success, joy and visibility. Calendula is also an herb of the ancestors and is used to honor the dead, and its golden petals brighten solar festivals like Litha and Lughnasadh.
medicalUses: Calendula is a beloved traditional skin healer. Infused oil and salves of the petals were used for cuts, scrapes, rashes, chapped skin, mild burns, nappy rash and insect bites. Its tea was used as a mouthwash for inflamed gums and as a gentle wash for sore eyes and skin.
whereToFind: Native to southern Europe and the Mediterranean; grows readily from seed in any sunny garden bed and self-seeds freely. Pick the flower heads when fully open, every few days, to keep them blooming, and dry on screens. Dried petals and calendula salves are sold at apothecaries and health food stores.
uses: Hang a garland of calendula over the door to keep evil out
Scatter petals under the bed for protection and prophetic dreams
Carry petals in your pocket on a court date
Make a calendula-infused oil for chapped hands and minor scrapes
Add petals to a solar ritual bath for joy and success
Offer the flowers on an ancestor altar
caution: Calendula can cause allergic reactions; avoid it if you are allergic to the daisy family (ragweed, chrysanthemum, marigold, chamomile). Avoid internal use during pregnancy and breastfeeding, as safety has not been studied. Patch test infused oils and salves before wider use. Do not confuse it with French or African marigolds (Tagetes), which are not used the same way.
interactions: No specific interactions are documented; in theory, large internal amounts may add to sedative medicines.

name: St. John's Wort
description: A sunny, star-flowered herb whose leaves, held to the light, appear pricked with tiny holes. Crush a yellow bud and it bleeds a crimson oil, which folk said was the blood of St. John the Baptist. Gathered at Midsummer and hung over doors and beds, it was called Fuga Daemonum, 'that which drives away demons.'
metaphysicalUses: St. John's Wort is the Midsummer herb of light. Gather it on Midsummer's Eve or St. John's Day and hang it over doors and windows to ward off ghosts, necromancers, evil spirits and lightning. Wear it to strengthen willpower and courage in battle, and to drive away fevers and melancholy. Burn it to banish spirits, and carry it to keep the soul bright through the darkening year. It is the classic herb of Litha.
medicalUses: Traditionally the bright red infused oil was applied to wounds, burns, bruises, nerve pain and aching muscles. The herb has long been taken to lift low spirits and the heaviness of winter; modern research supports some use for mild to moderate low mood, but it interacts with many medicines and should only be taken under professional guidance.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and Asia and naturalized widely (often considered a weed), growing in sunny meadows, roadsides, clearings and dry fields. Harvest the flowering tops around Midsummer when the buds are just opening and bleed red when squeezed. Dried herb and infused oil are sold by apothecaries and herb suppliers.
uses: Gather at Midsummer and hang over doorways to banish evil
Wear a sprig for courage and willpower
Make a red sun-infused oil in a clear jar for bruises and sore muscles
Burn a pinch to drive away lingering spirits
Add to Litha bonfires and solar altar decorations
Carry in a charm bag to keep melancholy away in winter
caution: Do not take internally without consulting a healthcare provider: it interacts with many medications, reducing their effectiveness or, with antidepressants, causing potentially dangerous serotonin syndrome. It should not replace treatment for depression. It causes photosensitivity, so avoid strong sun and tanning after use, including after applying the infused oil to the skin. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and stop at least 2 weeks before surgery. Burn only in a well-ventilated room, away from babies, pets and anyone with asthma, and never leave it smoldering unattended.
interactions: Weakens hormonal birth control, warfarin, digoxin, cyclosporine and other transplant drugs, HIV drugs, some cancer drugs and many others by speeding their breakdown; can cause serotonin syndrome with SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans and other serotonergic drugs.
pets: St. John's wort is listed by the ASPCA as toxic to dogs, cats and horses (sun sensitivity and skin inflammation); it is especially dangerous to grazing livestock.

name: Vervain
description: A slender, wiry herb with tiny lilac flowers, once so sacred that Roman priests swept their altars with it and Druids gathered it at the rising of the Dog Star with offerings of honey. Christian legend says it staunched Christ's wounds on the cross. It is the very archetype of the enchanter's herb.
metaphysicalUses: Vervain is one of the most versatile magical herbs. Use it to consecrate tools and altars, add it to purification baths, and hang it over the bed to prevent nightmares. Bury it in the garden or field for abundance and prosperity, wear it as a crown during spells for protection, and add it to love charms and peace-making rites. A home sprinkled with vervain-infused water drives away evil, and in hoodoo it is a key herb in Van-Van oil for luck and road opening. Vervain is a natural ally to anyone stepping into a magical path.
medicalUses: Traditionally a bitter, relaxing nervine used to ease nervous tension, restlessness, tension headaches and sleeplessness, and to support digestion and recovery after illness. It was also used to help nursing mothers and as a gentle tonic for exhaustion.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and the Mediterranean and naturalized widely, growing on dry roadsides, waste ground and sunny banks. Harvest the flowering tops in midsummer and dry them. Seeds are available from herb seed companies; dried vervain from apothecaries and witch shops. Do not confuse with lemon verbena or ornamental verbenas.
uses: Sweep your altar with a vervain bundle to consecrate it
Sprinkle vervain water around the home to drive away negativity
Hang a sprig over the bed to prevent nightmares
Bury vervain in the garden for abundance
Wear a crown of vervain during spellwork for protection
Sip a gentle vervain tea to ease tension before meditation
caution: Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding; it has traditionally been used to stimulate the uterus, and animal studies show harm to the developing fetus. Large doses can cause nausea and vomiting, and it may occasionally cause stomach upset or skin rash. Vervain tea can reduce iron absorption, so do not drink it with meals if you have low iron, and do not give it to infants.
interactions: May slow the liver's breakdown of some drugs (such as cyclophosphamide and barbiturates); check with a provider if you take liver-metabolized medicines.

name: Wormwood
description: A silvery, intensely bitter herb whose name in Revelation was given to a falling star that turned the waters bitter. It flavored the notorious green liqueur absinthe, the 'Green Fairy' of Parisian poets and painters. Legend says it sprang up along the path the serpent took when leaving Eden.
metaphysicalUses: Wormwood is burned in incense to increase psychic powers and is worn to protect against bewitchment and the attack of sea serpents. Hung from a car's rear-view mirror it is said to protect against accidents on dangerous roads. Burned in graveyards or with sandalwood, it is traditionally said to call spirits, so it is a classic Samhain and necromancy herb that should be handled with respect. It is also used in love divination and to send away anger.
medicalUses: Wormwood is one of the most bitter of all herbs and was traditionally used in very small doses as a digestive bitter to stimulate appetite and bile, and historically to expel intestinal worms (hence its name). It is strong medicine and was used only briefly and carefully by herbalists.
whereToFind: Native to temperate Europe, Asia and North Africa and naturalized elsewhere, growing on dry, waste ground, rocky slopes and roadsides. It is an easy, drought-tolerant perennial in full sun; harvest the flowering tops in late summer. Dried wormwood is sold by apothecaries and witchcraft suppliers; plants by herb nurseries.
uses: Burn a small amount with mugwort or sandalwood during Samhain spirit work
Hang a sprig in your car for protection on the road
Add a pinch to protection sachets against bewitchment
Plant it at the garden border to repel pests and unwanted energies
Lay dried wormwood on the altar during shadow work and ancestor rites
Tuck into stored woollens to deter moths
caution: Wormwood contains thujone, which is toxic to the nervous system in larger or prolonged doses and can cause seizures, kidney damage and convulsions; thujone content of supplements and oils is unpredictable. Do not use internally except briefly under qualified guidance, and never take the essential oil internally or combine it with other thujone-containing products (such as sage or thuja oil). Avoid completely in pregnancy (it may harm the fetus), breastfeeding, epilepsy and kidney or liver disease. People allergic to ragweed, chamomile or marigold may react. Burn only small amounts in a well-ventilated room, and keep it away from children and pets.
interactions: Interactions are not well studied; it could, in theory, lower the effectiveness of seizure medicines because thujone can provoke seizures.
pets: Keep wormwood and especially its oil away from dogs, cats and horses; thujone is toxic to animals too.

name: Rue
partsUsed: leaves (for charms and external ritual only)
description: A blue-grey, strong-smelling shrub with lacy leaves, called the Herb of Grace because Catholic priests once used rue branches to sprinkle holy water. It is the source of the Italian cimaruta, a silver charm shaped like a sprig of rue hung with symbols to guard against the evil eye. Few herbs are so steeped in protection lore.
metaphysicalUses: Rue is one of the strongest protective herbs against the evil eye, envy and hexes. Hang a sprig over the front door, grow it in the garden or a pot by the entry, and carry the cimaruta or a small sachet of dried rue to break curses. Rue wands and branches are used to sprinkle protective waters, and it is added to uncrossing and exorcism incenses (burned only in a ventilated space). In Latin American folk magic, ruda is placed in the home and on the altar for spiritual cleansing. Smelling fresh rue is said to clear the mind in matters of love.
medicalUses: Historically rue was used in European folk medicine for many ailments, but it is now recognized as too dangerous for home use. It is included here for its lore only; do not use it as a home remedy.
whereToFind: Native to the Balkans and Mediterranean, growing on dry, rocky, sunny ground. It grows well in pots or garden beds with full sun and lean soil; wear gloves and long sleeves when handling or cutting it. Plants are sold by herb nurseries; dried rue for charms is sold at botanicas and witchcraft shops.
uses: Hang a dried sprig over the front door against the evil eye
Grow a pot of rue by the entry as a living guardian (handle with gloves)
Wear a silver cimaruta charm for protection
Keep dried rue in a sealed sachet in a car or bag to break hexes
Use a sealed jar of rue on the altar during uncrossing work
Plant it at the garden edge to keep pests and envy away
caution: POISONOUS: rue is toxic when taken internally and can cause severe stomach pain, vomiting, liver and kidney damage, heart rhythm problems, and miscarriage. Contact with the plant or sap followed by sunlight causes severe blistering burns (phytophotodermatitis), even in children playing near it; always wear gloves and long sleeves when handling, and wash skin before going outside. Never ingest, never apply to skin, and avoid entirely in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Keep away from children and pets.
pets: Keep rue away from pets; ingestion can cause vomiting and contact can cause skin burns in sunlight.

name: Valerian
description: A tall herb with sweet, pale-pink flowers above a root whose earthy, musky smell is famously reminiscent of old socks. Cats adore it, and some say the Pied Piper of Hamelin carried valerian root to lure the rats. Galen called it 'Phu' for its smell, yet it has been a sleep herb since ancient Greece.
metaphysicalUses: Valerian root is used in protection sachets and hung in the home to guard against lightning and keep out evil. Its powdered root is added to purification incense, and in some old formularies it served as a stand-in for graveyard dirt. It is said to bring couples back together and calm quarrels, and to promote love when carried by a woman. Placed in a pillow it encourages deep sleep.
medicalUses: Valerian root is a classic traditional sedative, taken as a tea or tincture to ease sleeplessness, nervous tension, restlessness and anxiety. It was also used for muscle tension, menstrual cramps and tension headaches.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and Asia, naturalized in North America, growing in damp meadows, riverbanks and woodland edges. It grows easily in moist garden soil; dig the roots of two-year-old plants in autumn, wash and dry them. Dried root, capsules and tinctures are sold at health food stores and apothecaries.
uses: Place a small piece of dried root inside a sleep pillow
Hang valerian root over the door for protection
Add powdered root to a reconciliation spell for a quarreling couple
Drink a valerian and chamomile bedtime tea on restless nights
Add to purification incense (expect a pungent smell)
Offer a sprig to cat familiars, who often love it
caution: Can cause drowsiness, dizziness and reduced alertness; do not drive or operate machinery after use and do not combine with alcohol, sedatives or sleeping pills. Some people experience vivid dreams, headache, stomach upset or paradoxical stimulation, and stopping abruptly after long-term use can cause withdrawal-like symptoms. Rare cases of liver injury have been reported, so avoid with liver disease. Avoid in pregnancy, breastfeeding and in young children. Stop at least 2 weeks before surgery.
interactions: Adds to the effects of benzodiazepines, barbiturates, sleep medicines, opioids, alcohol and other sedatives; may affect drugs broken down by CYP3A4.

name: Lemon Balm
description: A soft, lemon-scented mint whose Greek name Melissa means 'honeybee,' for beekeepers rubbed it on hives to keep their swarms content. Paracelsus called it the elixir of life, and the Carmelite nuns distilled it into their famed Carmelite water. It gladdens the heart and chases away melancholy.
metaphysicalUses: Lemon balm is used in love spells and charms, and to attract friends and lovers. Steep it in wine and share it with someone special, or carry it to find love. Its cheerful, lunar energy dispels melancholy and is used in healing and success workings. Rub it on new beehives or offer it to bees to win their goodwill, and add it to baths for emotional healing and gentle self-love.
medicalUses: Lemon balm tea is a traditional gentle nervine for anxiety, restlessness, low mood and sleeplessness, and a soothing digestive for nervous stomachs and nausea. Topically, balm was dabbed on cold sores and insect bites.
whereToFind: Native to southern Europe, the Mediterranean and western Asia; naturalized in gardens, waste places and woodland edges. It self-seeds freely and grows easily in sun or part shade; harvest leaves before flowering and dry quickly to keep their scent. Plants are sold at garden centers and dried leaf at apothecaries and tea shops.
uses: Brew a lemon balm tea to lift the spirits on a grey day
Steep fresh leaves in white wine to share with a beloved
Add to a ritual bath for emotional healing
Plant near beehives or offer to the bees
Carry a sachet of balm to attract new friendships
Dab cooled strong tea on a cold sore
caution: Generally safe in tea amounts. It can cause drowsiness, so avoid driving until you know how it affects you and avoid combining it with alcohol. Laboratory studies suggest it may interfere with thyroid hormone signaling, so use caution with thyroid disease or thyroid medication. Little is known about safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so keep to moderate tea amounts.
interactions: May increase drowsiness with benzodiazepines, sleep medicines, opioids and other sedatives; may interfere with thyroid medication.

name: Hyssop
description: A bushy, aromatic Mediterranean herb with spires of deep blue flowers, beloved of bees. 'Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean,' sings Psalm 51, and hyssop has been a herb of spiritual washing ever since. In hoodoo it is the classic herb for cleansing away sin, guilt and spiritual filth.
metaphysicalUses: Hyssop is the most widely used purification herb of the Middle Ages and of hoodoo rootwork. It is added to baths to cleanse the spirit of sin, guilt and negativity, and the infusion is sprinkled on objects or people to purify them. Bundles of hyssop are hung in the house to drive out negativity and evil, and Psalm 51 is read while bathing in it. Hyssop is a gentle but powerful choice for spiritual cleansing after a crossing, a breakup or any heavy experience.
medicalUses: Traditionally a warming expectorant taken as a tea or syrup for coughs, chest colds, bronchial congestion and sore throats, and as a digestive for gas. It was also used as a gargle and a wash for bruises.
whereToFind: Native to southern Europe, the Middle East and the Caspian region, growing on dry, sunny, rocky slopes. Easy to grow in well-drained garden soil and full sun; harvest the flowering tops in summer. Dried hyssop is sold at apothecaries, botanicas and hoodoo suppliers.
uses: Take a hyssop bath while reciting Psalm 51 for spiritual cleansing
Sprinkle hyssop water on tools and objects to purify them
Hang a bundle in the house to drive out negativity
Add to uncrossing floor washes
Sip a hyssop and honey tea for a lingering cough
Plant near cabbages and beans to draw pollinators and repel pests
caution: Avoid in pregnancy (it has been used to bring on menstruation and miscarriage), breastfeeding, epilepsy and in young children. Hyssop essential oil contains pinocamphone and isopinocamphone, which have caused seizures in adults and children; never ingest the oil. Use the herb only in moderate tea amounts and for short periods.
interactions: May reduce the effectiveness of seizure medicines because the oil can provoke seizures.
pets: Keep the essential oil away from pets, especially cats; do not diffuse it where a cat cannot leave the room.

name: Patchouli
description: A bushy, soft-leaved mint of tropical Asia whose dried, fermented leaves give an earthy, musky, sweet scent that deepens with age. Victorian merchants packed Indian shawls in patchouli to deter moths, so the scent became the mark of a genuine import. Its smell is like rich soil after rain, and it smells of the earth's own fertility.
metaphysicalUses: Patchouli is an earthy herb of money, fertility and lust. Add it to money sachets and purses, sprinkle it on money, and anoint green candles with its oil to draw abundance. It is used in love sachets and baths for sensual attraction, and as a grounding scent in meditation. Patchouli's Saturnian earth energy makes it useful in binding work and is sometimes used as a substitute for graveyard dirt. Many modern witches anoint wallets and business cards with patchouli oil.
medicalUses: In traditional Asian folk medicine, patchouli was used for skin conditions, fungal infections and insect bites, and as an insect and moth repellent. The diluted oil is valued in aromatherapy for its grounding, calming effect.
whereToFind: Native to tropical Southeast Asia, grown commercially in Indonesia, India and the Philippines. It can be grown as a houseplant in warm, humid, bright conditions. Dried leaves are sold by herb suppliers and witch shops; essential oil at health food stores and apothecaries.
uses: Anoint a green candle with diluted patchouli oil for money drawing
Add dried leaves to a prosperity sachet in your wallet
Use patchouli in a sensual bath blend for attraction
Dab diluted oil on your wrists for grounding before meditation
Sprinkle on soil in a fertility or garden-blessing ritual
Tuck sachets in drawers to deter moths
caution: Undiluted patchouli oil can irritate the skin and cause allergic contact dermatitis; dilute it (a few drops in a carrier oil or lotion), patch test, and keep it out of the eyes. Do not ingest the essential oil. Little is known about safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so use cautiously.
interactions: Drug interactions are not well studied; ask a provider before combining with medicines.
pets: Keep the essential oil away from pets, especially cats; do not diffuse it where a cat cannot leave the room.

name: Sandalwood
description: The fragrant heartwood of a slow-growing, semi-parasitic tree of India, prized for millennia in temples, perfumes and carved sacred objects. In Hindu worship its paste marks the brow, and its scent clings to prayer beads for years. Its creamy, soft fragrance is said to carry prayers to the gods.
metaphysicalUses: Sandalwood has high spiritual vibrations and is burned at full-moon rituals, in meditation and to heighten spiritual awareness. Write a wish on a chip of sandalwood and burn it in a censer as you visualize it. Its powder is sprinkled for purification, sandalwood beads are used as protective prayer beads, and it is mixed with lavender to conjure spirits. Sandalwood is a superb base for incense blends of any purpose.
medicalUses: In Ayurvedic and folk traditions, cooling sandalwood paste was applied to the skin for rashes, heat and inflammation, and its scent used to calm the mind and ease anxiety. The diluted oil remains popular in skincare.
whereToFind: Native to southern India and parts of Southeast Asia and Australia, where it grows in dry deciduous forests. Indian sandalwood is endangered and heavily protected, so seek sustainably farmed Indian or Australian sandalwood (Santalum spicatum). Chips, powder and oil are sold at incense shops, Indian grocers and apothecaries.
uses: Write a wish on a sandalwood chip and burn it on charcoal
Burn sandalwood incense at the full moon for spiritual awareness
Use sandalwood mala beads in meditation
Sprinkle sandalwood powder on the altar to purify it
Add to any incense blend as a gentle, harmonizing base
Dab diluted oil on your third eye before meditation
caution: Generally safe diluted on the skin, but it can cause allergic skin reactions; patch test first. Do not ingest the essential oil; taken by mouth as medicine for more than about 6 weeks it may damage the kidneys, so avoid internal use with kidney disease, in pregnancy (it may increase miscarriage risk) and while breastfeeding. Choose sustainably and legally sourced sandalwood, as wild Indian sandalwood is overharvested and much on the market is adulterated. If burning on charcoal, do it only in a well-ventilated room on a heatproof surface, never in a closed space, because burning charcoal gives off carbon monoxide.
interactions: May raise lithium levels by acting as a diuretic.
pets: Keep the essential oil away from pets, especially cats; do not diffuse it where a cat cannot leave the room.

name: Frankincense
description: Pale golden 'tears' of resin bled from the bark of hardy desert trees in Arabia and the Horn of Africa. It was among the most precious goods of the ancient world, burned in the temples of Egypt, Babylon, Greece and Jerusalem and carried by the Magi to the infant Christ. Its smoke rises straight to heaven.
metaphysicalUses: Frankincense releases powerful vibrations when burned, raising the spiritual awareness of the practitioner and driving away evil and negativity. It is the classic resin for consecration and exorcism, burned to bless altars, tools and homes, and to prepare a space for meditation and prayer. Its sun energy brings success and confidence. It pairs with myrrh for a balanced blend of solar and lunar, masculine and feminine.
medicalUses: Frankincense resin has been chewed in Arabia for oral health and digestion, and burned as a fumigant. In folk and Ayurvedic tradition, Boswellia has been used for inflammation and achy joints. The diluted oil is used in aromatherapy to slow and deepen the breath and calm the mind.
whereToFind: Native to Oman, Yemen, Somalia and Ethiopia, growing on dry, rocky slopes. Many Boswellia populations are declining from overtapping, so buy from sustainable, fair-trade sources. Resin tears are sold at church supply stores, incense shops, apothecaries and witchcraft suppliers.
uses: Burn resin tears on charcoal to consecrate a new altar
Burn frankincense and myrrh together for spiritual balance
Smoke-bless new tools, jewelry and crystals
Burn before meditation or prayer to deepen focus
Add a tear to protection and success sachets
Anoint candles with diluted frankincense oil for sun magic
caution: Burn in a well-ventilated room; resin smoke releases fine particles that can irritate the lungs and pets' airways, and should be avoided around asthma, lung disease and infants. If burning on charcoal, do it only in a well-ventilated room on a heatproof surface, never in a closed space, because burning charcoal gives off carbon monoxide. Dilute the essential oil for skin use and patch test, since it can cause irritation, rashes and, rarely, blistering or allergic reactions. Avoid medicinal internal use in pregnancy and breastfeeding, as safety is unknown.
interactions: No well-documented interactions for frankincense resin; Boswellia supplements may interact with some medicines, so check with a provider.
pets: Keep smoke and the essential oil away from cats and birds; do not diffuse around cats.

name: Myrrh
description: A bitter, reddish-brown resin from thorny desert shrubs, prized since ancient Egypt for embalming, perfume and temple offerings. Greek myth tells of Myrrha, transformed into a tree whose tears became the resin and from whom Adonis was born. Myrrh was carried by the Magi as a gift foretelling death and resurrection.
metaphysicalUses: Myrrh is burned as incense to purify an area, raise vibrations and bring peace, and is added to healing incenses and sachets. It is almost always burned with frankincense to lend power and balance to any working. Myrrh is a lunar, ancestral resin associated with Isis, used in rites for the dead, grief work, initiation and consecration of tools.
medicalUses: Myrrh is a traditional antiseptic and astringent. Its tincture was used as a mouthwash and gargle for sore throats, mouth ulcers and inflamed gums, and applied to minor wounds and fungal skin infections.
whereToFind: Native to the Arabian Peninsula and the Horn of Africa, growing in dry, thorny scrubland. Resin is harvested by cutting the bark. Buy from sustainable sources at incense shops, apothecaries and church suppliers.
uses: Burn myrrh with frankincense to empower any ritual
Use myrrh smoke in rites for the dead and grieving
Add a resin piece to a healing sachet
Consecrate ritual tools in myrrh smoke
Anoint ancestor candles with diluted myrrh oil
Gargle with a few drops of myrrh tincture in water for a sore throat, then spit it out
caution: Avoid internal use in pregnancy (it may stimulate the uterus) and while breastfeeding. Do not take myrrh internally if you use warfarin, as it can weaken its effect.
