High doses may affect heart rate, and topical use can cause contact dermatitis, so avoid it on sensitive skin. For mouth use, gargle diluted tincture and spit it out. Burn in a well-ventilated room, and dilute the essential oil for skin use. If burning on charcoal, do it only in a well-ventilated room on a heatproof surface, never in a closed space, because burning charcoal gives off carbon monoxide.
interactions: May reduce the effect of warfarin (do not combine); may add to diabetes medicines by lowering blood sugar.
pets: Keep the essential oil away from pets, especially cats; do not diffuse it where a cat cannot leave the room.

name: Dragon's Blood
latin: Daemonorops draco; Dracaena cinnabari; Croton lechleri
description: A deep crimson resin from several unrelated trees: the rattan palms of Southeast Asia, the umbrella-shaped dragon trees of Socotra, and the South American Croton. Ancient sailors believed it truly was the blood of dragons slain by elephants. It has been used as a dye, varnish for Stradivarius violins, and a fiery potentiator in magic.
metaphysicalUses: Dragon's blood is the great amplifier: add a pinch to any incense to increase its potency. It is burned to drive out negative spirits and entities, carried for protection and good luck, and used to empower love spells. Women in Victorian folk practice burned it at an open window at night to bring back an absent lover. A stick placed under the bed is said to cure impotence, and its ink is used to write sigils, petitions and seals of power. In hoodoo it is a staple for both protection and commanding power.
medicalUses: The resins have been used traditionally as wound dressings and astringents. South American sangre de drago (Croton lechleri) sap is applied in Amazonian folk medicine to cuts, insect bites and skin conditions, forming a protective film. Other dragon's blood resins are now used mainly for incense.
whereToFind: Rattan dragon's blood is harvested from Daemonorops palms in Indonesia and Malaysia; Dracaena cinnabari grows only on the Yemeni island of Socotra and is vulnerable; Croton lechleri grows in the Amazon. Buy genuine resin chunks or powder (not dyed imitations) from incense shops, apothecaries and witch suppliers.
uses: Add a pinch of powdered resin to any incense to amplify it
Make dragon's blood ink to write sigils and petitions
Burn the resin to banish harmful spirits from a house
Carry a chunk in a red bag for protection and courage
Burn at an open window at night to call back an absent lover
Dress red candles with resin powder for power and passion
caution: Resin smoke can irritate the lungs; burn in a well-ventilated room away from children, pets and people with asthma. If burning on charcoal, do it only in a well-ventilated room on a heatproof surface, never in a closed space, because burning charcoal gives off carbon monoxide. Not for internal use. Many products sold as dragon's blood are synthetic or dyed, and safety data exist mainly for the Croton lechleri sap, so do not apply unknown resins or inks to broken skin. Stains skin, fabric and surfaces.

name: Copal
latin: Bursera spp.; Protium copal; Hymenaea courbaril
description: A fragrant, pale gold to amber resin burned in Mesoamerica for thousands of years. The Maya called it pom and the Aztecs copalli, 'incense,' offering it to the gods atop temple pyramids. It is still burned today on Día de los Muertos altars to guide the spirits of the dead home.
metaphysicalUses: Copal is a resin of purification and offering. Burn it to cleanse spaces, people and ritual tools, and as a sacred offering to ancestors, deities and spirits. It is the heart of many Day of the Dead and Mesoamerican ceremonies and is used in limpias (spiritual cleansings) by curanderas. Cunningham lists it for love and purification; a piece of copal can also stand in as a poppet heart. Its clean, bright smoke lifts the vibration of a room before any working.
medicalUses: In traditional Mesoamerican medicine, copal smoke was used in healing ceremonies and some copal resins were applied to the skin or used for respiratory complaints. It is used today chiefly as incense.
whereToFind: Native to Mexico, Central America and parts of South America, harvested by tapping the bark of copal trees. Buy from Mexican markets, botanicas, incense shops and fair-trade suppliers who source responsibly.
uses: Burn copal on Día de los Muertos altars to guide ancestors home
Cleanse the house with copal smoke on the new moon
Offer a small piece to your ancestors or deities
Smoke-cleanse crystals and ritual tools
Use a copal piece as the heart of a love poppet
Burn before divination to purify the space
caution: Burn in a well-ventilated room; incense smoke releases fine particles and irritants that can worsen asthma and other lung conditions, so keep it away from infants, pets and people with breathing problems. If burning on charcoal, do it only in a well-ventilated room on a heatproof surface, never in a closed space, because burning charcoal gives off carbon monoxide. Never leave burning resin unattended. Not for internal use.
pets: Keep smoke away from cats and birds, which have sensitive airways.

name: Benzoin
description: A vanilla-sweet, balsamic resin from Styrax trees of Southeast Asia, prized since medieval times as incense and as the base of Friar's Balsam. Its warm scent was used to fumigate homes against evil spirits in Malaysia and Indonesia. In incense crafting it is also a famous fixative that holds other scents together.
metaphysicalUses: Benzoin is burned as a purifier and is a frequent base of purification incense. Its smoke clears the mind and increases mental acuity, and in Mercurial and solar blends it aids focus and success. Benzoin, cinnamon and basil burned together attract customers to a business. It is also used to fix and preserve the scent of incenses and powders.
medicalUses: Benzoin tincture (as Friar's Balsam or compound benzoin tincture) was traditionally applied to small cuts and cracked skin as a protective antiseptic, and inhaled in steam for chest colds, coughs and congestion.
whereToFind: Native to Sumatra, Java, Thailand, Laos and Vietnam, harvested by tapping Styrax trees. Buy resin from incense shops, apothecaries and herb suppliers; benzoin tincture is available from pharmacies.
uses: Burn benzoin, cinnamon and basil to draw customers to a business
Burn before study for mental clarity
Add to homemade incense as a fixative
Use as a base for purification incense
Add a few drops of benzoin tincture to steam for a chest cold (adults only; take care to avoid scalds)
Smoke-cleanse your workspace on a Wednesday for focus
caution: Benzoin is a fairly common cause of allergic contact dermatitis; patch test before applying the resin or tincture to skin, and stop if redness or itching develops. Benzoin tincture is alcohol-based and flammable, so keep it away from flames. Use steam inhalations only for adults and older children, with care to avoid scalds. Incense smoke can irritate the lungs; burn in a well-ventilated room. If burning on charcoal, do it only in a well-ventilated room on a heatproof surface, never in a closed space, because burning charcoal gives off carbon monoxide. Not for internal use.
pets: Keep smoke away from cats and birds, which have sensitive airways.

name: Cedar
latin: Cedrus spp.; Thuja plicata; Juniperus virginiana
description: The name 'cedar' covers the great true cedars of Lebanon and the Atlas, as well as aromatic North American 'cedars' such as western red cedar and eastern red cedar. Solomon's temple was built of Lebanon cedar, Egyptians used its oil in mummification, and the Epic of Gilgamesh tells of a sacred cedar forest. Cedar smoke is also used in ceremonies by many Indigenous nations of North America.
metaphysicalUses: Cedar smoke purifies and is used to prevent bad dreams. A cedar stick hung in the home protects against lightning, and three small cedar pieces with points buried near the doorstep keep away evil. Cedar is placed in wallets and money jars to draw money, and kept in boxes to protect cherished items and magical tools. Its strong, long-lived wood lends steadiness and longevity to home blessings and ancestor work.
medicalUses: In folk practice, cedar oils were diluted and rubbed on the chest for congestion and used on the scalp and skin for dandruff and fungal problems. Cedar wood and chips have long been used to repel moths and insects.
whereToFind: True cedars grow in the mountains of the Mediterranean and Himalayas; western red cedar in the Pacific Northwest; eastern red cedar across eastern North America in fields and fencerows. Gather fallen twigs and needles respectfully. Cedar chips, wood and oil are sold at garden centers, pet stores, apothecaries and incense shops.
uses: Burn cedar tips to purify a home and prevent bad dreams
Keep magical tools and tarot cards in a cedar box
Place a cedar chip in your wallet to draw money
Hang a cedar stick in the home for protection
Add cedar to house-blessing incense
Tuck cedar blocks among woollens to keep moths away
caution: Thuja (arborvitae, sold as 'cedar leaf') contains thujone, which can cause seizures, vomiting and death in overdose, and is likely unsafe in pregnancy and breastfeeding; never take cedar or thuja oil internally. Dilute cedar oils for skin use and avoid them in pregnancy and with seizure disorders. Cedar smoke and sawdust can irritate the lungs and trigger asthma, so burn in a well-ventilated room.
interactions: Thuja may reduce the effectiveness of seizure medicines and immunosuppressants and may raise seizure risk with drugs such as bupropion or tramadol.
pets: Keep the essential oil away from pets, especially cats; do not diffuse it where a cat cannot leave the room.

name: Juniper
description: A prickly, blue-berried evergreen of heaths and mountainsides whose berries flavor gin. In Scotland, juniper was burned at Hogmanay in the 'saining' ritual to purify homes and livestock for the new year. European folklore says juniper sheltered the Holy Family, and in German lore it is the home of the gentle Frau Holle.
metaphysicalUses: Juniper is an ancient protective and purifying herb. Burn the branches and berries to cleanse a home in the Scottish saining tradition, especially at New Year, and hang a sprig by the door to guard against evil forces and thieves. Juniper berries carried attract lovers and increase male potency, and are used in healing and exorcism incense. A juniper smudge bundle is a beautiful local alternative to white sage across much of the Northern Hemisphere.
medicalUses: Juniper berries were traditionally used in small amounts as a digestive for gas and bloating and as a diuretic for water retention. Infused juniper oil was rubbed into aching joints and sore muscles.
whereToFind: Native across the Northern Hemisphere, growing on heaths, moors, rocky hillsides and open woodland. Pick ripe, blue-black berries (they take two to three years to ripen) in autumn, leaving plenty for wildlife. Dried berries are sold in spice shops; juniper shrubs at garden centers.
uses: Burn juniper branches at New Year to sain and bless the home
Hang a sprig over the door for protection against thieves
Carry juniper berries in a love sachet
Bundle juniper into smoke wands as a local sage alternative
Add crushed berries to protective incense
Cook with a few berries to aid digestion of rich game dishes
caution: Avoid in pregnancy (it may cause miscarriage) and while breastfeeding, and with kidney disease or inflammation, since large or prolonged doses can irritate the kidneys. Do not use medicinally for more than a few weeks, and never take the essential oil internally. It may affect blood sugar, so people with diabetes should monitor closely. Some juniper species (such as Juniperus sabina, savin) are toxic; use only Juniperus communis berries for culinary purposes. Burn branches only in a well-ventilated room.
interactions: May affect blood sugar control with diabetes medicines and, as a diuretic, may affect lithium levels and add to water pills.

name: Pine
description: The evergreen sentinel of northern forests, whose green needles promise life through the darkest winter. Pine was sacred to Attis and Dionysus, whose thyrsus wand was crowned with a pinecone, and the Haudenosaunee call the white pine the Tree of Peace. Bringing pine boughs indoors at Yule is a custom far older than Christmas.
metaphysicalUses: Pine is burned to purify and cleanse a home, especially in winter. Its boughs and needles are scattered on the floor to drive away evil and spread under the bed to keep illness away. Pinecones are carried to increase fertility and vigor in old age. Pine-needle baths cleanse and invigorate, and a cross of pine placed before the fireplace keeps evil from entering. Pine is also used in money spells, and its resin is burned at Yule for renewal and new beginnings.
medicalUses: Pine-needle tea, rich in vitamin C, was a traditional remedy against scurvy and winter colds, and pine steam and syrups were used for coughs and congestion. Pine resin salves were applied to splinters, sore muscles and small wounds.
whereToFind: Native throughout the Northern Hemisphere in forests, mountains and sandy soils. Gather fallen cones, needles and seeping resin from healthy trees without wounding them. Pine resin and oil are sold by incense and soap suppliers; needles can be foraged year-round.
uses: Burn pine needles or resin at Yule for renewal
Scatter needles across the threshold to drive away evil
Carry a small pinecone for fertility and vigor
Take a pine-needle bath to cleanse and invigorate
Brew a vitamin-rich pine-needle tea in winter (correctly identified species only, and never during pregnancy)
Add pine to money-drawing incense
caution: Never confuse pine with yew (Taxus), which is deadly, or with other lookalikes; only drink tea from a positively identified edible species such as eastern white pine. Ponderosa pine needles cause abortion in cattle and harmed pregnancies in animal studies, so avoid pine-needle teas entirely during pregnancy. Pine essential oil must be diluted and never swallowed; some people are allergic to pine resin (colophony). Burn needles or resin only in a well-ventilated room.
pets: Pine oil is toxic to cats; never diffuse it around them. Keep pets from chewing needles, which can upset the stomach.

name: Eucalyptus
description: A towering, silver-blue Australian tree whose leaves are rich in a cool, clearing oil. Aboriginal Australians used its leaves for healing for thousands of years, and koalas feed on little else. Its sharp, camphorous scent sweeps through the head like a cold wind.
metaphysicalUses: Eucalyptus is a healing herb. Its leaves are stuffed into healing poppets and sachets, and green candles ringed with eucalyptus leaves are burned for health. Hang a bundle in the shower to purify while bathing, and carry the leaves for protection. Eucalyptus is used to cleanse sickrooms of lingering illness and to clear the mind for fresh perspective.
medicalUses: Eucalyptus steam inhalations and chest rubs are classic folk remedies for colds, coughs, sinus congestion and bronchitis. The diluted oil was also used on aching muscles and as an antiseptic and insect repellent.
whereToFind: Native to Australia and Tasmania, now planted widely in warm regions such as California and the Mediterranean, where it can be invasive. Grows in pots in cooler climates. Fresh eucalyptus bunches are sold by florists and grocers; oil and dried leaves at pharmacies and apothecaries.
uses: Hang a bunch of eucalyptus in the shower to purify while bathing
Ring a green healing candle with eucalyptus leaves
Stuff leaves into a healing poppet for a loved one
Add 1 to 2 drops of oil to a steam bowl for a stuffy head (adults only; keep the oil and hot water away from children)
Cleanse a sickroom with eucalyptus after illness
Carry a leaf for protection when you feel run down
caution: Eucalyptus oil is poisonous if swallowed: a teaspoon or less can be fatal, and small amounts can cause seizures in children. Never swallow it, keep it out of children's reach, and do not use it on or near the faces of children under 2 or let children near vaporizer liquid. Dilute for skin and keep it out of the eyes. Avoid medicinal use in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
interactions: Medicinal amounts may lower blood sugar and add to diabetes medicines; the oil may change how the liver processes some drugs.
pets: Eucalyptus is toxic to cats, dogs and horses (drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, weakness); do not diffuse the oil around pets.

name: Elder
description: A shrubby tree of hedgerows and woodland edges, frothing with creamy blossom in early summer and heavy with purple-black berries in autumn. Folk across Europe believed the Elder Mother dwelt within it, and that one must ask her permission before cutting a single twig. To burn elder wood was thought to invite the devil, and to stand beneath it on Midsummer Eve was to see the faery king pass by.
metaphysicalUses: Elder is the witch's tree. Hang elder over doors and windows to keep evil out, and plant it near the home for protection. Wands made from elder wood are powerful for exorcising spirits and for faery magic, but always ask the Elder Mother's leave before cutting, and leave an offering. Elderflowers are scattered at weddings for blessing, and the leaves are traditionally carried against harm. Sit beneath an elder on Midsummer Eve to see the Fair Folk, and place its leaves under the pillow for peaceful sleep.
medicalUses: Elderflower tea, often with yarrow and peppermint, is a traditional remedy for colds, flu and fevers, bringing on a cleansing sweat. Properly cooked elderberry syrup is a folk favorite for coughs and winter immune support. Cooled elderflower water was used as a gentle skin wash.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa (with American elder, Sambucus canadensis, in North America), growing in hedgerows, woodland edges, riverbanks and disturbed ground. Pick flowers on dry sunny mornings in early summer and ripe, fully dark berries in late summer, always leaving some for birds. Dried flowers and berries are sold at apothecaries and health food stores.
uses: Ask the Elder Mother's permission, leave an offering, then cut a twig for a wand
Hang elder sprigs over doors and windows for protection
Make cooked elderberry syrup with honey for winter colds (never give honey to babies under 1 year)
Brew elderflower, yarrow and peppermint tea at the first sign of fever
Scatter elderflowers at a handfasting for blessing
Sit beneath an elder on Midsummer Eve to commune with the Fair Folk
caution: Raw or unripe elderberries, leaves, stems, bark and roots contain cyanide-producing compounds and can cause nausea, vomiting and severe diarrhea; always cook berries thoroughly and remove all stems. Use only black or blue elder; red elder (Sambucus racemosa) berries are more toxic. Little is known about safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Because elder may stimulate the immune system, consult a healthcare provider before use with autoimmune conditions or immunosuppressants. Never give honey or honey-based syrups to babies under 1 year old (risk of infant botulism).
interactions: May, in theory, counteract immunosuppressant drugs and add to the effects of diuretics and diabetes medicines.
